paragraphs: Feature importance methods assign importance to parts of an input to explain a neural network’s prediction. This paper asks how accurately those assignments identify important features. It introduces an empirical measure of approximate accuracy, providing a way to assess explanations rather than simply inspecting whether they appear persuasive.

Across several large image classification datasets, the authors find that many popular interpretability methods perform no better under this measure than assigning importance randomly. In the reported comparisons, only the ensemble methods VarGrad and SmoothGrad-Squared outperform that random reference. These findings concern the tested methods and the proposed evaluation measure; they do not establish that every use of feature importance is ineffective.

The paper also shows that combining multiple estimates does not automatically produce a better explanation. Some ensemble approaches add substantial computation without improving on their underlying method. The practical contribution is therefore both an evaluation tool and evidence that the particular way estimates are combined matters when judging explanation quality and computational cost.
neurips-2019-a-benchmark-for-interpretab.tldr: An empirical benchmark finds that many tested feature importance methods perform no better than random assignments, while certain ensemble methods improve.

paragraphs: Image captioning systems commonly use attention to connect image information with the words they generate. The paper challenges a fixed arrangement in which each output word receives one attended image feature vector. Describing an image can require more flexible relationships between visual regions and words, motivating a change to how attention proceeds during caption generation.

The proposed Adaptive Attention Time model learns how many attention steps to take before producing each word. This allows a word to attend to multiple image regions and allows an image region to contribute to multiple words. The central change is therefore the amount of attention computation associated with each decoding step, giving the system flexibility in how it aligns visual content with language.

The attention procedure is deterministic and differentiable, and the authors state that it introduces no noise into parameter gradients. Their experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art image captioning methods. These findings support adapting attention timing as a useful part of caption generation, alongside deciding which visual information should influence the next word.
neurips-2019-adaptively-aligned-image-ca.tldr: Adaptive Attention Time improves image captioning by learning how many attention steps to use when generating each word.

paragraphs: Emergent communication studies how agents develop a communication system because exchanging information helps them solve a task. In reinforcement learning tasks that unfold over time, learning this behavior without centralized training has been difficult. Part of the difficulty is joint exploration: speakers and listeners must discover useful communication behavior together.

The paper introduces inductive biases for positive signalling and positive listening. These are learning preferences intended to encourage the two sides of communication: producing informative signals and responding to messages. Addressing both sides matters because communication depends on a relationship between what one agent sends and how another agent uses it.

The authors first use a simple environment with a single step to demonstrate how these biases make learning easier. They then apply the approach to a longer environment, where agents equipped with the biases achieve better performance, and analyze the communication protocols that emerge. The findings provide evidence that encouraging signalling and listening can help agents overcome the coordination difficulties involved in learning to communicate.
neurips-2019-biases-for-emergent-communi.tldr: Learning biases that encourage signalling and listening help reinforcement learning agents develop useful communication in the tested environments.

paragraphs: Generating structured discrete objects presents two difficulties: an object may have many construction histories, and only some objects satisfy the domain’s validity rules. Learning across all possible histories can become intractable. The paper addresses these issues with a generative process built from local operations that preserve validity.

The model uses a Markov chain that alternates between corruption and learned reconstruction. Corruption produces objects that remain valid but depart from the data distribution. The reconstruction model then learns local changes that attempt to repair those corruptions while continuing to respect validity. This design restricts generated objects to valid ones and avoids summing over an unknown, potentially enormous collection of construction histories.

The authors evaluate the approach on molecules and Laman graphs, two domains with strong structural requirements. They report favorable comparisons with alternative methods in capturing distributional statistics across semantically relevant measures. The results support learning a sequence of valid local modifications as a way to model complex discrete objects while keeping their structural constraints built into generation.
neurips-2019-discrete-object-generation-.tldr: A generative Markov chain learns validity-preserving local repairs to produce structured discrete objects without enumerating their construction histories.

paragraphs: Neural network approximation theory can predict network sizes that grow sharply with data dimension, yet moderately sized networks often work well in practice. This paper investigates a proposed explanation: data may occupy a structure with far fewer dimensions than the surrounding input space. Its theoretical setting considers functions supported on low-dimensional manifolds.

The authors prove that neural networks can approximate such functions efficiently. The size requirement depends on the requested approximation accuracy, with an exponent determined by the data’s intrinsic dimension and the function’s smoothness. This identifies the dimension of the underlying structure as a key quantity in the approximation result and gives mathematical support to the value of exploiting that structure.

The work also implements a subnetwork that assigns inputs to their corresponding local neighborhoods. This supplies a concrete component for organizing computation around the manifold’s local structure. Together, the approximation result and neighborhood assignment construction help explain how low-dimensional organization can make function approximation more efficient, within the setting of functions supported on such manifolds.
neurips-2019-efficient-approximation-of-.tldr: The paper proves efficient neural network approximation for functions on low-dimensional manifolds, with size requirements governed by intrinsic dimension and smoothness.

paragraphs: Training a complex neural network can require retaining many intermediate values, making memory a bottleneck. Rematerialization addresses this by recomputing some values when they are needed instead of keeping them in memory throughout training. The central scheduling question is which values to retain and when to recompute the others.

The paper develops algorithms that use the structure of a network’s computation graph to answer that question. Specifically, it draws on structural characterizations called treewidth and pathwidth to construct rematerialization schedules with provable efficiency. These graph properties give the algorithms a way to organize the dependencies among intermediate computations when planning memory use and recomputation.

The authors also evaluate their algorithms on many common deep learning models. The contribution connects a practical training bottleneck with a graph-based approach to scheduling: the dependency structure of the computation becomes a resource for managing time and memory. Its theoretical guarantees and experimental evaluation address the same underlying task of deciding how to make effective use of limited storage during training.
neurips-2019-efficient-rematerialization.tldr: Graph-structural algorithms produce provably efficient schedules for recomputing neural network intermediates instead of storing them.

paragraphs: Images from physical experiments can have multiple plausible future states. In microstructure growth, for example, thermal fluctuations and environmental factors contribute to that variability. The paper studies how to generate diverse images from a conditioning image while also separating features associated with different sources of variation.

The proposed model, Flow U-Net with Squeeze modules, combines a flow-based image model with a U-Net-like architecture. The authors report that this combination captures probabilistic phenomena while retaining high image quality and diversity. It also automatically separates variation in target images into parts that depend on the conditioning image and parts that are independent of it.

Experiments cover microstructure growth and the CelebA dataset. The authors report that generated images outperform those of existing variational generative models in both quality and diversity. The contribution therefore joins conditional image generation with a distinction between two kinds of variability, addressing both the range of possible outputs and how that range relates to the supplied input image.
neurips-2019-flow-based-image-to-image-t.tldr: FUNS generates diverse conditional images while separating target variation into components that depend on the input image and components that do not.

paragraphs: Clustering a changing data stream involves more than finding a good solution once. When points can both arrive and disappear, an algorithm must maintain solution quality, update quickly, and avoid excessive changes between consecutive solutions. This paper studies those requirements in general metric spaces, focusing primarily on facility location.

The proposed algorithm maintains a constant-factor approximation with O(n log n) update time and O(n) total recourse, which measures changes to the maintained solution. Recomputing a solution at every step can instead require O(n²) update time and total recourse. The authors describe their bounds as nearly optimal, supported by the cost of specifying distances in general metric spaces and a recourse lower bound.

The approach also extends to k-median and k-means, maintaining constant-factor approximations with an update-time bound expressed as Õ(n + k²). Experiments show maintained solution costs very close to those obtained by quickly recomputing from scratch, with substantially better running time. The work makes stability across updates an explicit objective alongside clustering quality and computational efficiency.
neurips-2019-fully-dynamic-consistent-fa.tldr: A dynamic clustering algorithm maintains approximate solutions efficiently through insertions and deletions while limiting how much those solutions change.

paragraphs: Comparing graphs requires a way to assess differences in their structure. This paper approaches the problem through probability distributions of smooth signals defined on each graph. By comparing these distributions, the method accounts for global graph structure, addressing a weakness the authors identify in measures that examine local changes independently.

The authors derive an explicit Wasserstein distance between the signal distributions using graph Laplacian matrices. They then use this distance to define graph alignment: find a permutation of the nodes that minimizes the distance between two graphs. Because this alignment problem is non-convex, they propose an efficient stochastic algorithm that uses Bayesian exploration to search for a solution.

The framework is evaluated on graph alignment, graph classification, and graph signal prediction. The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art algorithms in these tasks. The contribution links a structurally meaningful graph comparison measure to an alignment procedure, allowing the same distribution-based view of graph structure to support several different types of graph analysis.
neurips-2019-got-an-optimal-transport-fr.tldr: GOT compares graphs through optimal transport between graph-signal distributions and uses the resulting distance to align their nodes.

paragraphs: Distributed neural network training must coordinate workers while limiting communication. Leader Stochastic Gradient Descent combines each worker’s ordinary gradient step with a correction toward the currently best-performing worker. This leader supplies a shared direction without requiring the algorithm to broadcast every worker’s parameters.

The paper identifies several advantages over the parameter-averaging method EASGD. Its objective preserves the original problem’s stationary-point locations, and the updates avoid slowing workers by pulling together parameter sets that are descending toward different local minima. The authors also design the correction to break symmetry associated with poorly generalizing, suboptimal solutions and provide theoretical analyses of both batch and stochastic versions.

An asynchronous implementation extends the idea to multiple leaders. Workers receive corrections toward both their group’s best performer and the best performer overall. Groups correspond naturally to workers within a computing node, while the global leader coordinates across nodes. Experiments training convolutional neural networks compare favorably with state-of-the-art baselines, supporting this combination of local progress, leader guidance, and reduced communication.
neurips-2019-leader-stochastic-gradient-.tldr: Leader SGD guides distributed workers toward the best-performing worker, combining gradient updates with communication-efficient coordination.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression when the fitted function must be convex and the observed data distribution may be perturbed adversarially. It proposes a nonparametric estimator for multiple input dimensions. Rather than choosing a fixed formula for the regression function, the method optimizes over convex functions using absolute prediction error.

The objective minimizes the worst error across Wasserstein perturbations of the empirical distribution. The authors solve this inner worst-case optimization in closed form, obtaining a regularization penalty involving the gradient norm. This connects robustness to changes in the observed distribution with a penalty on how strongly the fitted function varies with its inputs.

The authors prove consistency and a convergence rate of Õ(n^(-1/d)), matching stated bounds for alternative estimators based on squared loss. Their guarantees do not require a compact underlying domain or advance bounds on the convex function or its gradient norm. The result combines a robust estimation objective with convergence theory that avoids these particular restrictions on the domain and function.
neurips-2019-multivariate-distributional.tldr: A robust convex regression estimator turns worst-case distributional perturbations into gradient regularization and achieves convergence guarantees without compact-domain assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper asks what kinds of binary classification functions arise from random, wide, deep ReLU networks on bit-string inputs. It proves a preference for simple functions using two concrete notions of how much an input must change before its classification changes. The claim concerns this specified random-network setting.

For an input string of length n, the average Hamming distance to the nearest differently classified string is at least sqrt(n / (2π log n)). Hamming distance counts differing bit positions. The second result considers random bit flips: the average number required to change the classification grows linearly with n. Both statements describe average behavior, rather than a guarantee about every individual network or input modification.

Numerical experiments on networks with two hidden layers confirm the theoretical results. The authors connect this characterization to PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds, where the distribution of functions generated by random networks can serve as a prior. Understanding that distribution’s preference for simplicity contributes to explaining generalization by clarifying what functions the architecture favors before learning.
neurips-2019-random-deep-neural-networks.tldr: Random wide deep ReLU classifiers favor simple bit-string functions, as shown by average distances and random bit flips needed to change classifications.

paragraphs: Graph generative models must represent relationships among nodes and uncertainty about their hidden representations. The paper introduces SIG-VAE to expand the flexibility of variational graph autoencoders. Its hierarchical framework enables information sharing among neighboring nodes and uses a Bernoulli-Poisson link decoder in a model designed for sparse graphs.

A central feature is an inference network that propagates both graph structure and distributional uncertainty. The resulting semi-implicit hierarchical inference can represent complex posterior shapes, including heavy tails, multiple modes, skewness, and dependencies. This flexibility matters because uncertainty about a graph’s hidden representation need not fit a simple distribution, and neighboring nodes may carry related uncertainty.

The authors report that SIG-VAE outperforms straightforward combinations of a graph variational autoencoder with semi-implicit inference or normalizing flows that do not propagate uncertainty through the inference network. They also report more interpretable latent representations than VGAE and significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across several graph analysis tasks. The findings emphasize the joint design of graph generation and uncertainty-aware inference.
neurips-2019-semi-implicit-graph-variati.tldr: SIG-VAE improves graph generative modeling by sharing structural information and uncertainty through a flexible hierarchical inference network.

paragraphs: A pretrained neural network can transfer well to a new labeled dataset, but adaptation becomes harder when the target dataset has no labels. This paper investigates whether part of that difficulty comes from network architecture. It focuses on normalization as a component that could be changed to improve transfer between domains.

The authors introduce Transferable Normalization, or TransNorm, as a replacement for existing normalization techniques. It is a layer trained together with the rest of the network and is intended for use across different neural architectures and domain adaptation methods. The proposed replacement introduces neither extra hyperparameters nor additional learnable parameters, making its contribution an architectural change without expanding those sets of choices.

Empirical results show improved classification accuracy and faster convergence for mainstream deep learning domain adaptation methods. These findings support normalization design as a useful way to improve transfer in the tested settings. The paper presents architectural limitations as a possible source of weak transfer, rather than establishing them as the sole explanation.
neurips-2019-transferable-normalization-.tldr: TransNorm replaces normalization layers to improve unlabeled-target domain adaptation accuracy and convergence without adding learnable parameters or hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Models learned from limited, noisy data can make errors, so safety-critical control requires a way to quantify those errors. Gaussian process regression supports uncertainty estimates, and uniform error bounds can support safe control across a domain. This paper develops such a bound under weaker assumptions than those required by existing bounds.

The derivation combines the Gaussian process distribution with continuity arguments. The authors also use that distribution to obtain probabilistic Lipschitz constants, which describe how quickly a function can vary with its input under a probabilistic guarantee. They analyze the asymptotic behavior of the error bound, extending the work beyond its derivation to its behavior in the limit.

The paper then derives safety conditions for controlling unknown dynamical systems using Gaussian process models. Simulations of a robotic manipulator evaluate those conditions. The contribution links uncertainty quantification to concrete control requirements: a learned model supplies predictions, while the bound helps characterize when those predictions can support the stated safety conditions under the framework’s assumptions.
neurips-2019-uniform-error-bounds-for-ga.tldr: A Gaussian process error bound derived under weaker assumptions supports probabilistic regularity estimates and safety conditions for learned control.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network to reproduce a larger teacher’s predictions. This paper addresses the situation in which the teacher’s training data are unavailable. It proposes transferring the teacher’s behavior without access to any data or metadata, using generated images to provide training inputs.

An adversarial generator searches for images where the student’s predictions poorly match the teacher’s. Those images then train the student to reduce the disagreement. The generator thus directs training toward discrepancies between the two networks, making teacher-student mismatch the source of useful examples rather than relying on an available dataset.

The student closely approximates its teacher on simple datasets such as SVHN. On CIFAR10, the authors report outperforming the state of the art for few-shot distillation using 100 images per class, despite using no data. They also introduce a measure of prediction agreement near decision boundaries and observe significantly greater agreement for their student than for a student distilled with real data. This last finding concerns that specific boundary-focused measure.
neurips-2019-zero-shot-knowledge-transfe.tldr: An adversarial generator finds teacher-student disagreements and uses them to distill a smaller network without access to data or metadata.

paragraphs: Graph neural network analysis often asks whether two different graphs receive distinguishable representations. This paper asks a more graded question: how similar should their representations be? It focuses on neighborhood aggregation, where many popular networks combine neighboring attributes before applying a learned transformation.

The authors propose transform-sum-cat as an alternative aggregation scheme, using kernel distance to reflect continuous similarities between node neighborhoods. This leads to Weisfeiler-Leman similarity, or WLS, a graph similarity measure described as simple and efficient. The authors also emphasize that WLS is easy to implement using common deep learning frameworks, connecting the similarity construction to practical neural network development.

In graph classification experiments, transform-sum-cat significantly outperforms aggregation methods from popular graph neural networks. A simple, fast network built around it also achieves higher node classification accuracy, lower graph regression error, and more stable adversarial training for graph generation than widely used models in the reported comparisons. The results support designing aggregation around degrees of neighborhood similarity, alongside the ability to distinguish structures.
neurips-2020-a-graph-similarity-for-deep.tldr: A kernel-inspired aggregation scheme captures graded graph similarity and improves several graph learning tasks in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting human judgments of image quality is difficult. Hand-designed measures remain attractive for their speed and simplicity, while stronger learned measures can depend on costly class labels or quality ratings. This paper develops a learned perceptual quality measure using unsupervised training on pairs of video frames.

The proposed Perceptual Information Metric, or PIM, combines information-theoretic training objectives with an architecture informed by human visual physiology. The approach brings together a learning objective and a perceptually motivated computational design, while avoiding the supervised labels used by the compared modern approaches. Video frame pairs supply the material from which the metric is learned.

PIM is competitive with supervised metrics on the BAPPS image quality assessment dataset and performs better at predicting the ranking of image compression methods in CLIC 2020. The authors also conduct qualitative experiments on ImageNet-C and report robustness to architectural details. The findings show that an unsupervised training approach can yield a useful perceptual metric, with the strength of the reported comparison varying by evaluation task.
neurips-2020-an-unsupervised-information.tldr: PIM learns perceptual image quality from unlabeled video frame pairs and competes with supervised metrics on the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples can sometimes transfer between neural networks, making an example crafted against one model useful against another. This transferability supports many attacks in which the target network is not directly accessible. The paper investigates whether increasing linearity in an appropriate part of the computation can improve that transfer.

The proposed method, linear backpropagation or LinBP, changes how gradients are calculated for existing gradient-based attacks. The network’s forward computation proceeds normally. During backpropagation, however, the loss is propagated as though some nonlinear activations had not been encountered. This separates the model’s actual prediction computation from the modified backward computation used to construct adversarial examples.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show that LinBP outperforms state-of-the-art methods for crafting transferable examples and yields more effective attacks against a variety of networks. The reported evidence supports this particular way of increasing linearity during backpropagation. It connects the broader hypothesis about linearity and transferability to a concrete modification that works with existing attack methods.
neurips-2020-backpropagating-linearly-im.tldr: LinBP improves adversarial transfer in experiments by keeping forward predictions unchanged while treating some nonlinear activations as absent during backpropagation.

paragraphs: Inverse problems seek hidden system parameters that would produce specified measurements. The paper views deep inverse models as different ways of searching the space of possible solutions. From that perspective, it argues that evaluation should track accuracy over time, since judging only one proposed solution misses the behavior of the search process.

The authors compare several leading approaches on four benchmark tasks, including a new two-dimensional sinusoid task and metamaterial design. They also evaluate the neural-adjoint approach: train a neural network to approximate the forward system, then backpropagate with respect to its inputs to search for parameters that produce the desired output. The learned forward model supplies the gradients used during this search.

Adding a new boundary loss dramatically improves neural-adjoint performance in the reported evaluation. With this addition, the method achieves the best or nearly best results in every benchmark scenario. The contribution combines a time-dependent evaluation perspective with evidence that a comparatively simple surrogate-and-search method can be highly competitive on these inverse problems.
neurips-2020-benchmarking-deep-inverse-m.tldr: Time-based benchmarking shows strong inverse-problem performance from neural-adjoint search through a learned forward model, especially with an added boundary loss.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model events occurring in continuous time. Combining them with recurrent neural networks provides flexibility, but recurrence makes computation inherently sequential. This limits how much such models can benefit from modern parallel hardware, particularly when generating event sequences.

The paper introduces TriTPP, a non-recurrent class of temporal point process models built using developments in normalizing flows. Both sampling and likelihood computation can run in parallel. The authors report that TriTPP matches the flexibility of recurrent approaches while allowing sampling that is several orders of magnitude faster. The architectural change therefore targets the computational organization of event modeling while retaining expressive modeling capabilities.

Fast sampling also enables the authors to use TriTPP for variational inference in systems whose states are discrete but evolve in continuous time. Synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate advantages of the framework. The contribution links parallel event generation to a broader inference application, showing how removing sequential computation can expand the practical uses of a temporal point process model.
neurips-2020-fast-and-flexible-temporal-.tldr: TriTPP uses non-recurrent, flow-based temporal point processes to parallelize likelihood computation and achieve much faster sampling.

paragraphs: Mutual information summarizes average dependence between random variables, but an aggregate cannot describe the dependence associated with a particular pair of outcomes. This paper focuses instead on point-wise dependency, which quantifies how likely two outcomes are to occur together. The distinction changes the estimation target from an overall relationship to an outcome-specific one.

The authors show that point-wise dependency can arise naturally when optimizing neural variational bounds on mutual information. In practice, however, those optimization objectives can have large variance, making them difficult to use. To address this problem, the paper introduces two alternatives, Probabilistic Classifier and Density-Ratio Fitting, that avoid optimizing the mutual information variational bounds.

The proposed approaches are evaluated in mutual information estimation, self-supervised representation learning, and cross-modal retrieval. The authors report effectiveness across these applications. This demonstrates that estimating dependency at the level of individual outcomes can support both aggregate information estimation and tasks involving learned representations or relationships across modalities, while providing alternatives to the difficult variational-bound optimization route.
neurips-2020-neural-methods-for-point-wi.tldr: Two neural methods estimate outcome-specific dependency without optimizing high-variance mutual information bounds, supporting estimation, representation learning, and retrieval.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using historical data collected under another policy. Off-policy learning uses such data to select a policy with high expected reward. This paper addresses an additional difference: the covariate distribution in the evaluation data may differ from the historical distribution.

The authors derive an efficiency bound for off-policy evaluation under this covariate shift. They then propose doubly robust, efficient estimators for evaluation and learning that use an estimated density ratio between the historical and evaluation covariate distributions. This ratio provides a way to account for the distribution change when targeting expected reward on the evaluation data.

The paper also examines alternative estimators and compares their theoretical properties, then reports experiments confirming the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution makes the evaluation population explicit: performance is assessed for the data distribution where the new policy is meant to operate, while using experience gathered under both a different policy and a different covariate distribution.
neurips-2020-off-policy-evaluation-and-l.tldr: Density-ratio-based estimators support efficient, doubly robust policy evaluation and learning when historical and evaluation covariate distributions differ.

paragraphs: Automated machine learning searches over choices such as neural architectures and hyperparameters. The paper identifies a software obstacle: changing the search space, search algorithm, or larger search procedure often requires substantial changes to program logic. Complex arrangements, such as architecture search nested inside hardware configuration search, make those dependencies especially cumbersome.

PyGlove addresses this through symbolic programming. Machine learning programs become mutable objects that another program can manipulate, allowing automated search to operate through symbolic changes. This separates the search algorithm, search space, and program being searched. The framework supports changing algorithms with or without weight sharing, adding search to existing code, and composing more elaborate search procedures.

The authors introduce a Python library implementing this approach and present case studies on ImageNet and NAS-Bench-101. They show users converting static programs into search spaces, iterating on search definitions and algorithms, and building complex search flows to obtain better results. The main contribution is a programming model that makes these parts of automated machine learning easier to change and combine.
neurips-2020-pyglove-symbolic-programmin.tldr: PyGlove makes machine learning programs symbolically mutable so search spaces, algorithms, and complex search flows can be changed more easily.

paragraphs: Videos contain visual, audio, and language streams that can provide supervision for one another. This paper uses those naturally available modalities to learn representations without labeled training videos. Its goal is a versatile network that can accept multiple modalities and provide useful representations for downstream tasks across them.

The authors investigate how to combine the streams while retaining detailed visual and audio representations and incorporating text into a shared embedding. They also introduce a process called deflation, which allows the networks to be applied to either videos or static images. These choices address versatility both across types of information and across forms of visual input.

Networks trained on large collections of unlabeled video are applied to video, video-text, image, and audio tasks. Compared with previous self-supervised work, the learned representations achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks, including UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics600, AudioSet, and ESC-50. The findings support learning from video’s multiple streams as a route to representations useful beyond a single modality or task.
neurips-2020-self-supervised-multimodal-.tldr: Self-supervised learning from video, audio, and language produces versatile representations for video, image, audio, and cross-modal tasks.
